raw_content: {"cards":[{"title": "Cold Email Structure: Opener and Value in One Message", "summary": "Email outreach is more compact than DM, so the opener and the value offer should ship in the same email, kept personal, important-looking outside and personable inside.", "use_when": "Writing the first cold outreach email to a store owner, brand founder or marketing lead you want to work with or partner with.", "steps": ["Recognize that email, unlike Instagram DMs, is a compact channel — you do not get a separate 'opener' message and a later 'value' message with this prospect. Send both at once.", "Make the outside look important and worth opening: curiosity-based subject line that includes their first name so it reads as personal rather than spam.", "Write the inside as personal, witty and personable — not a dry, robotic pitch.", "End the email with a single strong value offer that is easy to say yes to (a short video, a free asset, a small low-risk project), so the reply step requires almost no effort.", "Warm the domain gradually over a long period rather than blasting volume immediately, so future emails don't land in the spam folder."], "caveats": ["The source frames this for service outreach; the structure transfers to supplier, affiliate and wholesale-partner emails, but the value offer must be something the other party actually wants."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "cold-email", "outreach", "subject-lines", "offer-design", "email-deliverability"]}, {"title": "Different Is Better Than Better in Cold Outreach", "summary": "Everyone in a prospect's inbox is sending the same dry 'we'll get you X in 60 days' pitch, so the winning move is being different and witty rather than marginally better.", "use_when": "Designing the angle and creative format for a cold outreach email to a brand or retailer, when your pitch otherwise looks identical to every competitor's.", "steps": ["Look at what the standard pitch in your space looks like — typically a dry claim about views, revenue or results with a conditional guarantee — and treat that as the boring baseline you must not match.", "Build the angle around your specific DNA, experiences and stories rather than around generic claims, since you are the one-of-one element no competitor can copy.", "Use creative devices that break the pattern: a small personalized graphic, a witty line, a funny image, or a Loom video email as the value vehicle.", "Keep all the underlying principles intact (personalization, justification for claims, easy reply CTA) — different is only better when the substance holds up."], "caveats": ["This is the presenter's strong opinion on cold outreach; he explicitly says it only works alongside the rest of the principles taught. The same creative move sent to a different niche or personality type may miss — some recipients respond to witty, others find it dumb."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "cold-email", "outreach", "creative-strategy", "positioning"]}, {"title": "Borrowed Authority Email: Make an Established Brand the Proof", "summary": "Instead of asking a prospect to trust your judgment, point at a top player in their niche already doing the thing you recommend and position yourself as the path to matching them.", "use_when": "Writing a mid-sequence outreach email or PDP/email critique to a store owner who has no reason yet to trust your recommendations.", "steps": ["Identify a brand or operator in the prospect's own vertical that is visibly ahead of them and that they already recognize as an authority.", "State the gap concretely: what the prospect's page, emails or funnel currently do versus what the top player's version does.", "Frame the recommendation as a route to copying a known winner rather than as your personal opinion: 'the same systems used by [top player]'.", "Give a short, low-friction CTA — offering a recorded walkthrough or sample asset they can review.", "Keep the email shorter and straighter than a witty anti-pitch email; borrowed authority is a proof angle, so it does not need jokes."], "caveats": ["Use a relevant, genuinely comparable authority figure — if the example is not someone the prospect respects or recognizes, the borrowed trust never lands."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "cold-email", "outreach", "social-proof", "positioning", "creative-strategy"]}, {"title": "Straight-to-the-Point Outreach Email With Permission to Say No", "summary": "A three-to-six line email that respects the prospect's time, adds risk reversal and explicitly gives permission to decline, which lowers pressure and often raises replies.", "use_when": "Prospect is busy or senior, or you have tried longer/wittier outreach and want a no-frills variant for your email sequence.", "steps": ["Open with an explicit time-respect line such as 'I value your time so I'll get straight to the point'.", "State what you made and the time cost to the recipient: a Loom video, a short walkthrough, roughly three minutes.", "Say what it will do for them in outcome terms (more conversions from the same traffic, more revenue with zero extra work).", "Add risk reversal so saying yes costs them nothing.", "Close with an easy micro-commitment and a pressure-release: reply 'yes' and you'll send it, and 'if not that's cool too, just let me know'.", "Skip wit and jokes in this variant — it is the straight version, meant for buyers who respond to brevity."], "caveats": ["Not a universal winner — the source presents this as one angle among several because different business owners respond to different tones."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "cold-email", "outreach", "risk-reversal", "subject-lines"]}, {"title": "Breakup Email: Create Scarcity With the Last Message", "summary": "A follow-up framed as the final email that tells the prospect you are about to delete the asset you made for them; the source reports this format generates a very high volume of replies.", "use_when": "A prospect has gone cold after several outreach emails and you are choosing which final follow-up to send before stopping.", "steps": ["Acknowledge directly that they've gone cold and that this is the last email on the subject.", "State a concrete, near-term consequence to the asset: you'll be taking down the Loom video shortly after sending this.", "Remind them what the asset covers — for example improvements to their headline or funnel that should lift conversions.", "Give one frictionless reply instruction: reply 'yes' and it's sent over.", "Keep the tone gracious rather than needy: if not, wish them luck with everything."], "caveats": ["The source calls this the strongest reply-getting follow-up but the claim is anecdotal; the threat must stay plausible — deleting an asset you genuinely would remove — or it reads as a bluff."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "cold-email", "outreach", "follow-up", "scarcity", "offer-design"]}, {"title": "Follow-Up Is the Neglected Half of Outreach", "summary": "The source argues follow-up matters as much as or more than the initial outreach and that inconsistent, un-followed-up outreach is the real reason people conclude outreach doesn't work.", "use_when": "Scheduling your outreach cadence and deciding how many touches a prospect should receive before you stop, or when someone has replied but hasn't converted.", "steps": ["Treat follow-up as a designed part of the sequence, not an optional add-on: plan multiple touches over time.", "Come back from different angles each time (a new proof point, a different creative format, a different offer framing) rather than repeating the same message.", "If a prospect replied at any point, do not let them go — a reply proves they are open to the offer once the timing is right.", "Push discipline over cleverness: the failure mode is people completing steps only partially and then blaming outreach.", "Accept that first attempts feel clunky and may not land a client immediately; the fix is completing the sequence and improving, not switching methods."], "caveats": ["The presenter states this forcefully from his own experience as an agency owner; no numeric reply rates are established, so treat the intensity as his opinion, not a measured benchmark."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "follow-up", "outreach", "cold-email", "experiment-design"]}, {"title": "Video Intro DM: Send Video or Voice Note Instead of Text", "summary": "Stand out from text-only DMs by sending a short video (or voice note) that introduces you on camera, states how you help, and offers either a call or free value.", "use_when": "Instagram or social DM outreach to a brand or store owner, especially when most competitors are sending plain-text pitches.", "steps": ["Open with a normal opener as you would for a text DM — warm and specific.", "Instead of writing out your value pitch, record a short video or voice note introducing who you are, what you do, and how you can help them.", "At the end of the video pitch either the call ('if that's something you'd be open to, let me know and we can hop on a call') or the value ('I made a longer walkthrough / sample email sequence — say the word and it's in your inbox in minutes').", "In the thumbnail or first frame, put their name on the video so they can see it was made for them specifically.", "Look presentable and speak articulately — the source says the on-camera competence is itself the social proof and authority signal.", "Keep the script extremely simple; the presenter states his own script feels too simple to work and it still gets results."], "caveats": ["Voice notes work but are explicitly stated to be less effective than video. This directly answers the biggest objection — whether you can sound like them — and if the emails are good they may simply use them, making you the writer going forward.", "Free sales page example: produce a document showing what their sales page copy would look like if you wrote it, so they evaluate actual copy rather than a description of your service.", "Loom funnel audit: record a walkthrough of their funnel with alternatives and proof behind each claim.", "Combine assets when useful — the presenter sometimes writes a free sales page and records a Loom contrasting their current page with the rewrite.", "Before choosing the asset, listen to what the prospect asks for; in the case study the prospect himself listed sequences he needed (event ticket sales, upsell, welcome/nurture, revival), which made the follow-up easy to scope."], "caveats": ["These are the presenter's own closing examples from his practice; they show what worked for him, not guaranteed results. The work is free up front — you only convert if the quality holds."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "outreach", "value-offer", "cold-email", "product-page", "email-sequence", "loom"]}, {"title": "Answering Budget and Trust Objections With a Low-Risk First Project", "summary": "Agree with the objection first, then shrink the scope to a small paid test project so the store can judge your work without a large commitment.", "use_when": "A prospect says your quoted price is over budget or that they won't commit big without first seeing your quality — common on retainer or full-funnel quotes.", "steps": ["Agree with the objection immediately ('totally understandable — that's a big commitment without seeing what I can do'); never argue that the deal is already good value, since that creates friction.", "Reframe yourself as the one qualifying the fit as well: 'see if we're a good fit to work together' rather than 'let me show you how good I am'.", "Propose a single small low-risk project with a concrete deliverable and price — in the case study, one eight-email sequence for $400 when the prospect balked at a ~50–60 email project. the lesson is about personalization, not about banning automation tooling itself."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "outreach", "dm-outreach", "personalization", "cold-email"]}, {"title": "Set Up Your Social Profile So the Prospect Pitches You", "summary": "A profile showing what you do and who you've helped can turn a bare opener into the prospect asking to buy before you ever pitch.", "use_when": "Preparing your social profile before starting DM outreach so that your opener does the minimum and the profile does the selling.", "steps": ["Define your bio around three things: what you do, how you do it, and who you've helped before.", "Keep the opener minimal — the case study opener was just a general compliment ('love the real estate and wealth gems'), which the presenter admits wasn't specific.", "Let the profile carry the pitch: in that case the prospect replied asking about email copy pricing without the sender ever mentioning copywriting.", "Note the counterpoint: the presenter says if he repeated the outreach he would write a better, more specific opener — the profile covers the gap, but a specific opener is still stronger.", "Apply the same principle to your storefront equivalents — profile, pinned content, and public portfolio links — since they are legible the moment someone checks who messaged them."], "caveats": ["The source's example is personal-brand DM outreach, not ecommerce; change the phrasing drastically so your message doesn't look like something the prospect has already seen.", "use_when": "Using any outreach template or swipe file for ecommerce partner or brand outreach before sending it.", "steps": ["Make a personal copy of every template file you use — in Google Drive, use File > Make a copy rather than requesting access — so your edits stay yours.", "Treat the template's structure (opener, proof, value offer, CTA, permission to decline) as the reusable part.", "Rewrite the words: change the phrasing, the specific reference, the joke and the deliverable, so it reads as written for this recipient.", "Recognise that templates widely shared on the internet circulate to the same prospects; a verbatim send signals you're a beginner and makes the prospect unwilling to work with you.", "Keep the specificity check: a line that works for a sales coach ("I've been watching your sales advice, it helped me close a deal") is wrong for a fitness or dating coach — the idea travels, the words don't."], "caveats": ["The presenter shares many templates himself and acknowledges that even with volume, duplication is likely; Some prospects delegate DMs to salespeople, so be ready to be routed."], "tags": ["ad-copy-deployment", "outreach", "dm-outreach", "social-selling", "follow-up", "video-outreach"]}, {"title": "Warm List-to-Email Handoff: Be Ready With Sample Work and Portfolio", "summary": "When a DM contact routes you to a manager or inbox, be prepared to hand over email samples and a portfolio immediately — that handoff is often what converts.", "use_when": "You are doing social outreach to a brand and they ask you to email someone internally, or they request work samples.", "steps": ["Expect the handoff: a DM reply like 'too busy, email this person' is a path forward, not a rejection.", "Have email samples ready to send the moment they ask, so the conversation doesn't stall on your production time.", "Maintain a portfolio link and be ready to say what other copy you write — in the case study the request was specifically for portfolio plus non-email copy types.", "Offer to discuss small projects as the next step, framing it as seeing whether you're a good fit rather than pushing for the biggest scope.", "Expect practical steps like NDAs and briefs, and keep moving — the same case study closed a 10-email sequence at $2,000 with around 30–40 minutes of work per email."], "caveats": ["The $2,000 / 10-email figure is a specific case study, not a rate card.
